1177.title: The wide permitted
1177.hook: most of life is simply permitted
1177.howItsDone: Muslim jurists generally start from permission in food, trade and everyday life, asking for evidence before calling something forbidden, while acts of worship follow what was taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahkam, the five rulings, a dial and not a switch. Your line: five kinds of acts.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells the people that Allah has made the pilgrimage a duty for them. A man calls out: every year, Messenger of Allah? The Prophet stays silent. The man asks again, and again. Finally the answer comes, in Sahih Muslim: if I said yes, it would become a duty every year, and you would not be able to do it. Then a request: leave me as I leave you. Don't go hunting for burdens nobody placed on you. Today's word is the space that request protects.
screen: `EVERY YEAR, MESSENGER?` → `SILENCE.` → `LEAVE ME AS I LEAVE YOU.`

segments.voice: The word is mubah, permitted, the middle of yesterday's dial. No reward for doing it, no blame for leaving it. Jurists have a principle about it that changes how the whole law feels: in things and in dealings, the starting point is permission. Something is permitted unless a text forbids it, not the other way round. The Qur'an says, in Surah al-Baqarah: "He it is Who created for you all that is in the earth." For you. The food, the trade, the clothes, the games, the jokes, the long walk at dusk. Jurists start from yes, and ask for evidence before they say no. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari puts the warning sharply. The Prophet says the Muslim with the greatest guilt is the one who asks about something that wasn't forbidden, and it becomes forbidden because of his asking. Asking isn't the problem in that report. Inventing burdens is. Now one turn, so this isn't misread. The starting point flips for worship. Jurists say a new act of worship needs a text behind it, because worship is offered the way it was taught. In prayer, start from what was taught. In the market, the kitchen and the park, start from permitted. Put those together and the forbidden becomes a list, and the permitted a wide field. A person can spend most of a day in the field, eating, working, laughing, resting, and none of it is outside the law. Some of it can even become worship, jurists add, when it's done with a good intention.
screen: `MUBAH: SIMPLY PERMITTED.` · `THE STARTING POINT IS YES.` · `DON'T INVENT BURDENS.` · `WORSHIP STARTS FROM WHAT WAS TAUGHT.`

segments.voice: Choose something small that's simply allowed, a cup of tea, bread still warm, the sound outside your window, a stretch, and do it now, or hold it in your mind. Don't turn it into a task; let it be a good thing in the wide field. If you pray, you can thank Allah for it.
Mubah. Permitted: no reward for doing it, no blame for leaving it, and in things and dealings, the starting point. Today's word.
Your line: most is permitted. A good thing, in the wide field, with no permission slip needed. Go gently.

1178.title: Striving to understand
1178.hook: a qualified scholar's effort to reach a ruling
1178.howItsDone: Qualified jurists, known as mujtahids, derive rulings from the Qur'an, the sunnah and the other sources; Shia Muslims turn to living mujtahids, and Sunni scholars work largely within the established schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mubah, the wide field of the permitted. Your line: most is permitted.

News reaches a town: something about safety, or something about danger, and people pass it along at once, before anyone has checked what it means. The Qur'an, in Surah al-Nisa', describes that scene. If they had referred the matter to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, it says, the ones among them able to draw it out would have known it. Draw it out. Some answers don't sit on the surface. Someone has to go down after them, and the going down takes work, and training, and honesty about what you find. Today's word is that work.
screen: `NEWS PASSED ON UNCHECKED.` → `THOSE ABLE TO DRAW IT OUT.` → `SOME ANSWERS LIE DEEP.`

segments.voice: The word is ijtihad, striving, exerting yourself to the limit. In law it names a qualified scholar's full effort to reach a ruling from the sources. Everything this block has laid out is the toolkit: the Qur'an, the sunnah, agreement, analogy, reason, the common good, custom. Ijtihad is the work of picking them up and using them on a real question. Earlier in this block came a report in Sahih al-Bukhari about two judges who both strive: the one who gets it right has two rewards, and the one who misses has one. That striving has a name, and this is it. Notice the word qualified. The one who does ijtihad, the mujtahid, is expected to know the Qur'an and the sunnah closely, to know Arabic well, to know where the scholars already agree, and to know the method. That's why the reward for being wrong isn't a loophole for anyone with an opinion. It's for the person who did the work. And here the communities differ. Some later Sunni writers spoke of the door of ijtihad as closed, with the great questions settled inside the schools; other Sunni scholars argued the door never closed. Among Shia Muslims, living mujtahids remain at the center of religious life, and believers turn to them for rulings today. That's tomorrow.
screen: `IJTIHAD: STRIVING TO THE LIMIT.` · `TWO JUDGES, BOTH REWARDED.` · `ONLY THE QUALIFIED.` · `IS THE DOOR OPEN?`

segments.voice: Pick one real question, small but honest: should I say yes to this, what do I owe this person? Go in order, the way the schools teach it: what do the things I trust most say, what has someone wise already done, and only then, my own best judgment, with full effort. You may still get it wrong; the effort is the point.
Ijtihad. Striving: a qualified scholar's full effort to reach a ruling from the sources. Today's word.
Your line: effort to understand. The reward is for the one who did the work. I'll be here tomorrow.

1179.title: Following a scholar
1179.hook: most people follow a qualified scholar or school
1179.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims may follow one of the established schools of law, often the one their teachers or region follow; Shia Muslims follow a living marja' al-taqlid and consult that jurist's book of practical rulings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ijtihad, a qualified scholar's full effort. Your line: effort to understand.

Who taught you how to tie your shoes? Not a theory of knots. A person, who knew, and showed you, and you trusted them. Now a harder question. A Muslim misses a day of the Ramadan fast while traveling. How exactly is it made up, and by when? A mujtahid can work that out from the sources. But what about the nurse, the bus driver, the student, who has never studied legal theory and never will? The Qur'an, in Surah al-Nahl, tells its hearers to ask the people of the reminder if they do not know. Today's word is what happens next.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU YOUR SHOELACES?` → `A MISSED FAST, MADE UP HOW?` → `ASK, IF YOU DO NOT KNOW.`

segments.voice: The word is taqlid, following: taking a ruling from a qualified scholar without working out the evidence yourself. Some teachers explain it with a picture from the word's root, a qiladah, a necklace or collar: the follower places the question around the scholar's neck, and the scholar carries the answer. In Sunni communities, taqlid means following a school: the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi'i or the Hanbali. A family in one region may pray by Hanafi rulings because their teachers did, and a family in another by Shafi'i ones. In Shia communities, believers follow a living jurist, called a marja' al-taqlid, a source to follow. A marja' publishes a book of practical rulings, and a believer can open it and look up the missed fast, the travel prayer, the question about work. Both communities draw a line around it. Taqlid is for the practical rulings. Jurists in both communities have taught that the core beliefs, God's oneness, the prophethood, are a matter of a person's own understanding, not borrowed. And taqlid has its critics. Some Sunni voices urge believers to follow the evidence directly rather than a school, and others reply that knowing the evidence well is exactly what the schools were built for. The debate is old and still going. What taqlid isn't is laziness. It's the same trust as the shoelaces, placed carefully: in someone qualified, someone trustworthy, someone whose method is known. The question a follower asks isn't whether to trust. It's who.
screen: `TAQLID: FOLLOWING ONE WHO KNOWS.` · `SUNNI: A SCHOOL TO FOLLOW.` · `SHIA: A LIVING SOURCE TO FOLLOW.` · `ONLY FOR PRACTICAL RULINGS.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, ask yourself who taught you to pray and whom they learned from; if you know your school or your marja', say the name quietly and remember one ruling you keep because of them. If you're not Muslim, ask whose guidance you follow on the things you haven't studied, and why you trust them. Then hold one teacher's face in mind.
Taqlid. Following: taking a practical ruling from a qualified scholar or school. Today's word.
Your line: follow one who knows. Trust, placed carefully, in someone qualified. Until tomorrow.

1180.title: Difference as mercy
1180.hook: a well-known saying calls scholarly difference a mercy
1180.howItsDone: Muslims of different schools pray and fast according to their own school's rulings side by side in the same mosques, and scholars study the reasons behind each school's view in a field called the study of disagreement.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taqlid, following a qualified scholar on practical rulings. Your line: follow one who knows.

An instruction goes out to a company of the Prophet's companions: none of you is to pray the afternoon prayer except at the settlement of Banu Qurayza. They set off, and the sun drops lower on the road. If they keep walking, the prayer's time will pass. One group says: he meant hurry, not miss the prayer, and they pray on the road. Another says: he said there, and they pray only when they arrive, late. Same words, two honest readings. In Sahih al-Bukhari, when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, hears about it, he blames neither group. Today's word is what happened on that road.
screen: `PRAY ONLY AT BANU QURAYZA.` → `THE SUN SINKS ON THE ROAD.` → `TWO READINGS, NEITHER BLAMED.`

segments.voice: The word is ikhtilaf: difference, disagreement, the scholars going different ways. People repeat a saying: the difference of my community is a mercy. It's quoted as a hadith, and here honesty matters. Hadith scholars have said they found no reliable chain for it back to the Prophet. The idea, though, is carried by other reports. A saying attributed to the caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz has him say he would not have been glad if the companions had never differed, because their difference left room for those who came after. And a story the biographies tell: a caliph wanted to make Imam Malik's book, al-Muwatta, the single law for every city. Malik declined. The companions had spread to different cities, he said, each carrying what they knew, and people should be left with what had reached them. Think back to the road: the same words, honest readings, neither group blamed. That's the picture of a mercy. Two schools can place the hands differently in prayer, and both be following their method faithfully. But this isn't difference about everything. It lives inside a shared ground: the oneness of God, the prayer, the fast, the Qur'an. And it's reached by method, the method of the last two weeks: shari'ah and fiqh, the Qur'an and sunnah, agreement, analogy, reason, the common good, custom, the five rulings, the wide permitted, striving, following. That closes the foundations. Next, the schools themselves, one by one, beginning with the merchant of Kufa.
screen: `IKHTILAF: GOING DIFFERENT WAYS.` · `A SAYING WITH NO SOUND CHAIN.` · `MALIK WON'T MAKE ONE LAW.` · `DIFFERENCE INSIDE SHARED GROUND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a way someone else practices that isn't yours: some Muslims pray with arms folded and others with arms at their sides, each following their school, or a family that keeps a holiday differently from yours. Hold it without correcting it, and ask what honest reading might be behind it, like the two groups on the road. If you pray, you can pray for the one who differs from you.
Ikhtilaf. Difference among scholars, reached by honest method, held as a mercy. Today's word.

1181.title: Abu Hanifa
1181.hook: the Kufa scholar and merchant, known for honesty and careful reasoning
1181.howItsDone: Hanafi Muslims follow the school named for Abu Hanifa and carried by his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, and Hanafis honor him with the title al-Imam al-A'zam, the great imam.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the foundations with ikhtilaf, honest difference held as mercy. Your line: difference, mercy.

A heap of grain sits in the market. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, walks past and pushes his hand into it, and his fingers come out wet. The top is dry; the damp is hidden underneath. Rain, the seller says. Then why not put the wet part on top, the Prophet asks, where people can see it? And then, in Sahih Muslim, the line: whoever cheats is not of me. A new part of this year begins today, the schools of law, one by one, with a man who knew markets from the inside.
screen: `A HEAP OF GRAIN, WET UNDERNEATH.` → `WHOEVER CHEATS IS NOT OF ME.` → `A SCHOLAR FROM THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: His name was al-Nu'man ibn Thabit, and he's remembered as Abu Hanifa. He lived in Kufa, in Iraq, a city full of scholars and full of trade, and he earned his living selling cloth. He bought and sold, set prices, and dealt with customers who could be lied to. The biographies tell a story about it. Abu Hanifa gave his partner a garment to sell, told him it had a defect, and told him to point it out to the buyer. The partner sold it and forgot to mention it. When he found out, the story goes, he gave away the whole price of that sale in charity, because he couldn't keep money from a sale that hid something. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari reads almost like a commentary on it: when buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their sale is blessed; when they hide and lie, the blessing is wiped away. Then the scholar. The biographies say he taught in circles where students argued a question from every side before settling it. His method leaned on careful reasoning, and tomorrow looks at its tools. His students, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani among them, wrote down and carried the school that bears his name. A saying attributed to al-Shafi'i, founder of another school, calls people dependents of Abu Hanifa in law. The biographies also say he refused a post as a judge under the rulers of his time, and suffered for refusing. Hanafis call him al-Imam al-A'zam, the great imam. Honesty in the market, care in the argument: the school started with both.
screen: `AL-NU'MAN OF KUFA, A CLOTH MERCHANT.` · `THE GARMENT WITH A HIDDEN DEFECT.` · `TRUTHFUL AND CLEAR: A BLESSED SALE.` · `A CIRCLE THAT ARGUED EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of your next exchange, selling something online, splitting a bill, reporting your hours, and look for the wet grain under the dry: a scratch you'd rather not mention, a minute you'd round up. Picture putting it on top, where the other person can see it, and notice what that costs, and what it frees. If you pray, you can ask for an honest hand.

1182.title: Opinion and principle
1182.hook: the Hanafi method uses reasoned opinion and juristic preference
1182.howItsDone: Hanafi jurists reach rulings from the Qur'an and sunnah first, then use considered judgment and juristic preference, choosing a stronger proof over a plain analogy, in questions the texts leave open.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Hanifa, the merchant of Kufa, and your line: the great imam.

A fasting man forgets. It's the middle of a long day, there's water on the table, and he drinks before he remembers. Has he broken his fast? Follow a straight line of logic and the answer is yes: the fast means no drink, and he drank. But in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says whoever forgets while fasting and eats or drinks should complete the fast, because it was Allah who fed him and gave him drink. A story told about Abu Hanifa has him say that if it weren't for that report, he would have followed the logic. What do you call setting the obvious rule aside for a stronger reason? Today has two words for it.
screen: `A FASTING MAN FORGETS AND DRINKS.` → `THE STRAIGHT LINE SAYS: BROKEN.` → `THE REPORT SAYS: COMPLETE IT.`

segments.voice: The first is ra'y, opinion, but not the kind you shout across a dinner table. In law it means a considered judgment, reached by a trained mind where no text settles the question. In Kufa, Abu Hanifa and his circle used it so carefully, and so often, that critics called them the people of ra'y. Some meant it as a warning; the Hanafis took it as a description of hard work. And it keeps an order. A saying attributed to Abu Hanifa lays it out: the Book of Allah first, then the sunnah of the Prophet, then the sayings of the companions. Only after that did his own judgment begin. The second word is istihsan, juristic preference, often explained as counting one answer the better one. Sometimes a plain analogy points one way and a stronger reason points another: a report, a real hardship, the settled practice of people. Istihsan chooses the stronger reason, and the forgetful faster is a case Hanafi books give for it. Not everyone agreed. Al-Shafi'i, whom you'll meet soon on this path, wrote that preference without a text is a jurist pleasing himself. Hanafi scholars answered that istihsan is never a mood: it's a preference with a proof behind it, named and open to challenge. The two schools still disagree about the word, and both say the texts come first.
screen: `RA'Y: A CONSIDERED JUDGMENT.` · `THE BOOK, THE SUNNAH, THEN THE MIND.` · `ISTIHSAN: CHOOSING THE STRONGER REASON.` · `AN ARGUMENT OVER ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Pick a small decision where both answers are decent: call your mother tonight or visit this weekend, finish the work or rest. Hold each side and name its reason plainly, the obvious rule on one side and any stronger reason on the other, someone's need, a promise, a cost you hadn't counted, as if you had to explain it to a fair friend. 1183.title: His students
1183.hook: Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani spread the school
1183.howItsDone: Hanafi law books record the views of Abu Hanifa beside those of his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, and later Hanafi jurists weigh all three when deciding the school's position.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ra'y, a considered judgment, and istihsan, choosing the stronger reason. Your line: reasoned preference.

In the classic Hanafi law books, a strange habit shows up again and again. A ruling is given, and then: Abu Hanifa said this, but Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said that. The founder, contradicted by his own students, on the same page of the school's own book. Nobody tore the page out. Nobody threw the students out. Their names sit beside his, and sometimes later Hanafi scholars even follow the students' view over the teacher's. An odd way to honor a teacher, until you see what the students were doing.
screen: `ABU HANIFA SAID THIS.` → `HIS STUDENTS SAID THAT.` → `ON THE SAME PAGE.`

segments.voice: The first is Abu Yusuf. He sat in Abu Hanifa's circle in Kufa and later served as a judge for the Abbasid caliphs. For the caliph Harun al-Rashid he wrote Kitab al-Kharaj, a book on taxes and the public treasury, giving the school's reasoning a place at court. The second is Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani, the great writer of the pair. His books set down the school's positions in order, and Hanafi scholars came to treat a set of them as the school's core record. They say much of Abu Hanifa's teaching reached later readers through what these two wrote. Hanafi books call the three the imams of the school, and the students the two companions. When the companions disagreed with their teacher, they said so, and the books kept every view. For a school built on reasoned judgment, that fits. A student who repeats a teacher's answers carries the answers. A student who learned the method can carry the method, even past the teacher. So the week closes: most of life simply permitted, ijtihad, taqlid, difference as mercy, Abu Hanifa and his ra'y, and now the people who made sure any of it survived. A school isn't one man. It's a teacher, and students honest enough to argue with him, and to write it all down.
screen: `ABU YUSUF: THE JUDGE AT COURT.` · `AL-SHAYBANI: THE WRITER.` · `THE TWO COMPANIONS DISAGREE ON THE PAGE.` · `A WEEK OF METHOD, CARRIED ON.`
